record.original_question: Let A be a nonnegative tensor of order m and dimension n. Define the majorization matrix by M(A)_{ij} = a_{ij...j}. For a fixed j in [n], call A j-primitive if there exists a positive integer k such that (M(A^k))_{u j} > 0 for every u in [n]. Call A irreducible if there is no nonempty proper subset I of {1, ..., n} such that a_{i_1...i_m} = 0 whenever i_1 is in I and i_2, ..., i_m are all outside I. Is it true that A is primitive if and only if A is irreducible and there exists some j in [n] for which A is j-primitive?

evidence.quote: The majorization matrix M(A) of the tensor A is defined as (M(A))ij = aij...j, i, j in [n].

For a fixed integer j in [n], if there exists a positive integer k such that (M(A^k))_{u j} > 0, for all u in [n], then A is called j-primitive and the smallest such integer k is called the j-primitive degree of A, denoted by γ_j(A).

A tensor C = (c_{i1...im}) of order m dimension n is called reducible, if there exists a nonempty proper index subset I subset {1, . . . , n} such that c_{i1...im} = 0 for all i1 in I, for all i2, . . . im not in I. If C is not reducible, then we call C irreducible.
Conjecture 4.5. Let A be a nonnegative tensor with order m and dimension n. Then A is primitive if and only if A is irreducible and there exists some j in [n] such that A is j-primitive.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $m, n \geq 2$ be integers and let $A = (a_{i_1 i_2 \cdots i_m})_{1 \le i_1,\ldots,i_m \le n}$ be a nonnegative tensor of order $m$ and dimension $n$ (i.e., all entries $a_{i_1\cdots i_m} \ge 0$).

Define the majorization matrix $M(A)$ of $A$ to be the $n \times n$ nonnegative matrix with entries
$$ M(A)_{ij} = a_{i\, j\, j\, \cdots\, j}, \qquad i,j \in [n] := \{1,\ldots,n\}. $$
Powers $A^k$ of $A$ are defined via the standard tensor product so that each $A^k$ is again a nonnegative tensor of order $m$ and dimension $n$.

Definitions:
1. ($j$-primitivity) For a fixed $j \in [n]$, the tensor $A$ is called $j$-primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that
$$ \big(M(A^k)\big)_{u\,j} > 0 \quad \text{for every } u \in [n]. $$
2. (Irreducibility) The tensor $A$ is called reducible if there exists a nonempty proper subset $I \subsetneq [n]$ such that
$$ a_{i_1 i_2 \cdots i_m} = 0 \quad \text{whenever } i_1 \in I \text{ and } i_2,\ldots,i_m \in [n]\setminus I. $$
$A$ is irreducible if it is not reducible.
3. (Primitivity) $A$ is called primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that every entry of the majorization matrix $M(A^k)$ is strictly positive.

Question: Prove or disprove the following statement. A nonnegative tensor $A$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$ is primitive if and only if $A$ is irreducible and there exists some $j \in [n]$ such that $A$ is $j$-primitive.
artifact.status_search_result: Web searches for the conjecture characterizing primitivity of a nonnegative tensor as the conjunction of irreducibility and the existence of some j for which the tensor is j-primitive did not return a definitive resolution. Related work characterizes primitivity of nonnegative tensors via cycles in the associated directed hypergraph, and other conjectures on the primitive degree have been confirmed, but a clear published proof or counterexample of this specific equivalence was not located.

status_evidence.title: Primitive tensors and directed hypergraphs
status_evidence.snippet: Characterizes primitivity of nonnegative tensors via cycles in the associated directed hypergraph.
status_evidence.claim: Related characterizations of primitive tensors exist, but the specific equivalence is not directly confirmed.

status_evidence.snippet: Discusses Shao's conjecture on the primitive degree bound for nonnegative primitive tensors.
status_evidence.claim: A different conjecture about the primitive degree bound was confirmed, but this is not the same statement.
